idiom_name: EF Core owned type mapped to a JSON column: OwnsOne(...).ToJson()
implementation_notes: EF Core 7 and later map an owned aggregate to a JSON column with one call: modelBuilder.Entity<Order>().OwnsOne(o => o.Details, b => b.ToJson()); LINQ queries against the aggregate are translated into JSON drill-down and SaveChanges writes the whole document back, provider-agnostically. On older stacks, or when the payload has no .NET type inside the model, an explicit ValueConverter with System.Text.Json over a string column does the same work - supply a ValueComparer when the converted value is mutable, or change tracking will miss in-place edits. Keep the fields you filter or join on outside the JSON document; nothing inside it can carry a foreign key or constraint.
pitfalls: The aggregate is only visible through its owner: unsupported expressions fail query translation at runtime, and the JSON entity cannot be queried like a table.
A ValueConverter without a ValueComparer makes mutable payloads look unchanged (or always changed); the owned-type JSON mapping tracks the aggregate instead.
The document has no schema or version of its own - renames and splits need an explicit version field plus a backfill, because no migration covers the inside of the column.
